doc_description: Microsoft Corporation’s Form 10‑K for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2023, detailing its companywide push to embed responsible generative AI across products, strong cloud performance ($111.6B Microsoft Cloud; Azure +29%; $211.9B total revenue), segment results and risk factors, SOX 404(b) internal control attestation, shareholder returns, market risk disclosures, properties, legal proceedings, and exhibits.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- Microsoft Corporation’s Form 10-K annual report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2023, filed under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (Commission File No. 001-37845).
- Company details: incorporated in Washington (I.R.S. ID 91-1144442); principal office at One Microsoft Way, Redmond, WA 98052-6399; phone (425) 882-8080; investor website www.microsoft.com/investor.
- Securities registered under Section 12(b): Common stock ($0.00000625 par value), 3.125% Notes due 2028, and 2.625% Notes due 2033, all trading under symbol MSFT on NASDAQ; no securities registered under Section 12(g).
- Filing status and compliance: well-known seasoned issuer; large accelerated filer; not an emerging growth company; not a shell company; has filed all required reports and submitted all required interactive data files in the preceding 12 months.
- Internal control: includes management’s report on internal control over financial reporting and an auditor attestation under SOX 404(b).
- Market metrics: aggregate market value of non-affiliate common stock as of December 31, 2022 was approximately $1.8 trillion; 7,429,763,722 shares outstanding as of July 24, 2023.
- No indications of error corrections to previously issued financial statements or restatements requiring incentive compensation recovery analysis.
- Documents incorporated by reference: portions of the definitive Proxy Statement for the December 7, 2023 Annual Meeting (Part III).
- Table of contents outlines Part I–IV items, including: Business; Executive Officers; Risk Factors; Properties; Legal Proceedings; Market for Common Equity and Issuer Purchases; MD&A; Market Risk; Financial Statements and Supplementary Data; Changes in and Disagreements with Accountants; Controls and Procedures; Other Information; Disclosure Regarding Foreign Jurisdictions that Prevent Inspections; Directors and Governance; Executive Compensation; Security Ownership; Related Transactions and Director Independence; Auditor Fees and Services; Exhibits and Financial Statement Schedules; Form 10-K Summary; and Signatures.

structure.title: PART I
structure.heading: PART I
structure.start_phrase: This report includes estimates, projections, statements relating to our business plans, objectives, and expected operating results that are “forward-looking statements” within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, Section 27A of the Securities Act of 1933, and Section 21E of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
structure.summary:
- Forward-looking statements disclaimer: Defines forward-looking terms, points readers to Risk Factors, MD&A, and Market Risk sections, warns of risks and uncertainties, and states no obligation to update such statements.
- Company overview and mission: Microsoft aims to empower every person and organization globally, creating AI-powered platforms and tools to drive opportunity, growth, and impact across sectors.
- AI strategy and integration: Broad infusion of generative AI across products and services (e.g., Microsoft Teams, Outlook, Bing, Xbox) and “copilot” capabilities throughout the Microsoft Cloud to help customers innovate, optimize spend, and enhance security/management.
- Responsible AI principles: Commitment to fairness, reliability/safety, privacy/security, inclusiveness, transparency, and accountability.
- Offerings and business model: Mix of software, services, devices, and solutions; cloud-based platforms and content; solution support and consulting; and online advertising.
- Product portfolio: Operating systems; productivity and collaboration apps; server and business applications; management and development tools; video games; and devices including PCs, tablets, gaming consoles, intelligent devices, and accessories.
- Strategic ambitions: (1) Reinvent productivity and business processes, (2) Build the intelligent cloud and intelligent edge platform, and (3) Create more personal computing.
- Productivity focus: Providing technology and resources to enable secure, productive work environments that support how people work, learn, and connect.

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: Item 1. Business
structure.start_phrase: Microsoft is a technology company whose mission is to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more.
structure.summary:
- Company overview and mission: Microsoft aims to empower people and organizations globally, with a company-wide focus on infusing AI across platforms and tools. Emphasis on responsible AI guided by principles of fairness, reliability/safety, privacy/security, inclusiveness, transparency, and accountability.
- Offerings: Broad portfolio of software, services, devices, solutions, and online advertising. Cloud-based solutions span infrastructure, data, business applications, collaboration, and consumer services.
- Strategic ambitions:
  - Reinvent productivity and business processes.
  - Build the intelligent cloud and intelligent edge platform.
  - Create more personal computing.
- Reinvent productivity and business processes: Continuous innovation in Microsoft 365 (Office 365, Windows, Enterprise Mobility + Security), Teams, Viva, Dynamics 365, and LinkedIn; introduction of Microsoft 365 Copilot; low-code/no-code via Power Platform; LinkedIn as a professional network and talent/marketing/sales/learning platform.
- Intelligent cloud and edge:
  - Azure as a global-scale, hybrid-consistent cloud with economies of scale, developer productivity, AI, and trusted security/compliance.
  - Azure AI platform enabling enterprise-grade, responsible AI; accelerating intelligent edge (IoT to edge hardware).
  - Partnership with OpenAI (exclusive cloud provider; deploying models across products; investment in AI supercomputing).
  - Security, compliance, identity, and management integrated across hybrid environments; industry clouds; Azure Arc for multi-cloud/on-prem governance.
  - Nuance acquisition: conversational AI and ambient intelligence, notably in healthcare and other industries.
  - Mixed reality with Microsoft Mesh; data platforms including Microsoft Intelligent Data Platform and Microsoft Fabric; developer tools (GitHub Copilot, Visual Studio).
  - Windows 365 (cloud PC) and Azure Orbital (ground-station-as-a-service).
- More personal computing:
  - Windows 11 with Windows Copilot, Dev Home, and enhanced security/privacy.
  - AI-powered Edge and Bing (including Bing Chat) to improve search, answers, and content generation.
  - First-party devices (Surface portfolio) to spur ecosystem innovation.
  - Gaming investments across content, community, and cloud (Xbox hardware, Game Pass, cloud gaming); broadening access across PC, console, and mobile; announced plan to acquire Activision Blizzard.
- Future opportunity priorities: Lead the next AI wave; deepen cloud value; transform work with modern modular business apps; end-to-end security across clouds/platforms; expand gaming experiences; use Windows to drive cloud engagement.
- Corporate social responsibility:
  - Sustainability: Commitments to be carbon negative, water positive, and zero waste by 2030; FY22 progress (overall emissions -0.5%, Scope 3 +0.5% and 96% of total; >13.5 GW carbon-free energy PPAs; 15.6M m3 water replenishment contracted; 12,159 metric tons waste diverted; 12,270 acres protected). Microsoft Cloud for Sustainability helps customers measure and reduce emissions.
  - Racial equity: Multi-year pillars—strengthening communities, engaging ecosystem, increasing representation/inclusion—targeting 2025 goals; progress across justice reform, broadband access, nonprofit tech acceleration, TEALS expansion; increased investments with Black- and African American-owned financial institutions/suppliers/partners; representation gains toward doubling leadership.
  - Digital skills: Skills for Jobs initiative; cybersecurity workforce program to help skill/recruit 250,000 in the U.S. by 2025 and expansion to 27 countries; AI Skills Initiative with LinkedIn learning pathway and grants for generative AI skilling.
- Human capital resources:
  - Workforce: ~221,000 employees (120k U.S., 101k international) across operations, R&D, sales/marketing, and G&A.
  - Culture and inclusion: Growth mindset; extensive employee listening systems; robust Employee Resource Groups; leadership accountability for culture/diversity with public reporting (representation, EEO-1, disability, pay equity).
  - Total rewards and pay equity: Market-competitive, performance-focused compensation; FY23 salaried base pay held at FY22 levels while maintaining stock and bonus programs; reported adjusted pay equity across gender and racial/ethnic groups; unadjusted median pay gaps disclosed with commitment to reduce over time.
  - Wellbeing and hybrid work: Comprehensive benefits and mental health support; hybrid flexibility guidance with strong employee satisfaction.
  - Learning and development: Global Viva Learning access; required compliance/culture training; profession-based skilling; >27,000 people managers with extensive compulsory leadership training.
- Operating segments:
  - Productivity and Business Processes: Office Commercial/Consumer, LinkedIn, Dynamics 365 and on-prem ERP/CRM; growth drivers include user expansion, ARPU, and cloud shift; competition from Apple, Cisco, Meta, Google, Slack, Zoom, Okta, Proofpoint, Symantec; LinkedIn competes with professional networks, HR tech, job boards, and ad platforms; Dynamics competes with Oracle, Salesforce, SAP.
  - Intelligent Cloud: Azure and other server products/services; Nuance and GitHub; Enterprise Services. Azure competes with Amazon, Google, IBM, Oracle, VMware, and open source; AI offerings compete with hyperscalers and open-source LLMs; server products compete with Unix/Linux ecosystems and numerous middleware/database/developer tool providers; Enterprise Services competes with global consulting firms and niche providers.
  - More Personal Computing: Windows (OEM and Commercial), Devices (Surface, HoloLens, accessories), Gaming (Xbox hardware/content/services, Game Pass, cloud gaming), Search and news advertising (Bing, Edge, Microsoft News, affiliates). Competition spans Apple/Google (OS/devices), Nintendo/Sony and major tech platforms (gaming/streaming), and Google/social platforms (ads).
- Operations: Global operations centers (U.S., Ireland, Puerto Rico) supporting sales/fulfillment; expanding datacenters to meet AI demand with dependencies on land, energy, networking, servers/GPUs; third-party contract manufacturing with some single/limited-source components posing supply risk.
- Research and development and intellectual property:
  - Engineering groups across Cloud & AI, Strategic Missions & Technologies, Experiences & Devices, Microsoft Security, Technology & Research, LinkedIn, and Gaming.
  - Large patent portfolio (>70,000 issued; >19,000 pending), active IP protection and licensing, and engagement with open source.
  - Microsoft Research as a major corporate research organization; global R&D footprint; ongoing significant investment in emerging technologies and long-term innovation.
- Distribution, sales, and marketing: Multiple channels—OEMs, direct (enterprise agreements, digital marketplaces, Microsoft Experience Centers), and distributors/resellers (LSPs, VARs, retailers); strong partner ecosystem for sales, consulting, and fulfillment.
- Licensing options: Volume licensing and cloud agreements including Enterprise Agreement, Microsoft Customer Agreement, Microsoft Online Subscription Agreement, Microsoft Products and Services Agreement, Open Value, and Select Plus; Software Assurance benefits; partner programs (Cloud Solution Provider, Services Provider License Agreement, ISV Royalty Program).
- Customers: Broad base spanning consumers to global enterprises and public sector; backlog not significant due to prompt shipment practices.
- Executive leadership: Listing of executive officers, including Satya Nadella (Chairman & CEO) and other EVPs; brief bios for Nadella and Judson Althoff included.

structure.title: Information about our Executive Officers
structure.heading: Information about our Executive Officers
structure.start_phrase: Our executive officers as of July 27, 2023 were as follows:
structure.summary:
- Overview of Microsoft licensing and purchasing programs:
  - Open Value: three-year agreements for small and medium organizations to license cloud and on-premises software; option for perpetual or subscription licenses; Software Assurance (SA) included.
  - Select Plus: designed for government and academic customers to buy perpetual on-premises licenses across affiliates/departments; SA optional.
  - Partner programs:
    - Cloud Solution Provider (CSP): partners package and manage Microsoft cloud subscriptions with their own services.
    - Services Provider License Agreement (SPLA): hosting providers/ISVs license eligible Microsoft software over three years; monthly billing based on consumption.
    - ISV Royalty Program: enables partners to embed Microsoft products into applications and license the combined solution.

- Customer base and sales practices:
  - Customers span consumers, SMBs, large enterprises, public sector, ISPs, developers, and OEMs.
  - Products are shipped promptly upon purchase orders; backlog not significant.

- Executive leadership (as of July 27, 2023):
  - Lists key executives: Satya Nadella (Chairman & CEO), Judson Althoff (EVP & CCO), Chris Capossela (EVP & CMO), Kathleen Hogan (EVP & CHRO), Amy Hood (EVP & CFO), Brad Smith (Vice Chair & President), Chris Young (EVP, Business Development, Strategy & Ventures).
  - Brief career histories and select external board roles.

- Investor and corporate information availability:
  - Investor Relations website provides SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K), strategy and financial metrics, event archives, earnings and product press releases, and corporate governance documents.
  - CSR Reports Hub features sustainability, responsible sourcing, accessibility, digital trust, and public policy reports.
  - Notes on website/social media communications and their potential materiality; clarification that web content isn’t incorporated by reference.

- Risk factors (strategic and competitive):
  - Intense competition across technology markets with low barriers to entry and rapid innovation cycles; need for continual product and service innovation.
  - Competition among platform ecosystems:
    - Vertically integrated competitors (hardware, software, services) can claim security/performance advantages; shifting toward vertical integration can increase cost of revenue and compress margins.
    - Windows PC licensing faces pressure from smartphones/tablets and low/no-cost operating systems; potential impact on developer interest and OEM relationships.
    - Importance of content/app marketplaces and developer support; user switching costs; competing marketplace rules may constrain distribution; efforts to compete may increase costs and reduce operating margins.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase: Our operations and financial results are subject to various risks and uncertainties, including those described below, that could adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of operations, cash flows, and the trading price of our common stock.
structure.summary:
- The excerpt is from Part I, Item 1A (Risk Factors) of a Form 10‑K and outlines extensive risks that could adversely affect the company’s business, financial condition, results, cash flows, and stock price.
- Strategic and competitive risks:
  - Intense competition across platform-based ecosystems and devices; pressure from vertically integrated competitors and free/ad-supported or open-source models.
  - Shifts from PC-centric Windows licensing to smartphones/tablets and competing app/content marketplaces may erode margins and developer engagement.
  - Rapidly evolving AI market requires heavy investment and responsiveness to technology, regulation, and public scrutiny.
  - Execution risks in scaling cloud services (Azure, AI, IoT), including pricing models, reliability, security, platform-agnostic delivery, and fraud/abuse on services.
- Business evolution risks:
  - Large, ongoing investments in products (Windows, Microsoft 365, Azure, Xbox, LinkedIn) and AI may not achieve expected returns; delays or quality issues can hurt revenue and margins.
  - M&A and strategic partnerships (e.g., gaming, healthcare AI, AI partnerships) pose integration, compliance, distraction, and return risks; potential goodwill/intangible impairments.
- Cybersecurity, data privacy, and platform abuse:
  - Sophisticated cyberattacks (including nation‑state and supply‑chain attacks), zero‑day vulnerabilities, account compromise, ransomware, and open-source dependencies.
  - New security risks from generative AI features; costly ongoing investment needed in secure engineering and update/mitigation capabilities.
  - Liability and reputational risk from personal data disclosure/misuse; constraints from government data requests and data localization.
  - Risks from scraping and misuse of platform content; content, advertising, marketplace, and gaming abuses (misinformation, impersonation) and increasing content moderation regulations.
  - IoT security, privacy, and safety challenges; AI bias, flawed models, harmful outputs, and emerging AI regulation (e.g., EU) may cause legal, ethical, or brand harm.
- Operational risks:
  - Service outages and data loss risks amid rapid scale-up of datacenters and AI workloads; dependencies on land, power (including clean-energy transition), GPUs/servers, and networking.
  - Hardware/software quality issues; supply chain constraints, component shortages, inventory risks; reliance on assembly and suppliers in higher-risk geographies.
- Legal, regulatory, and litigation risks:
  - Antitrust scrutiny in the EU, U.S., China; potential fines, product modifications, and constraints on acquisitions; coopetition with OEMs raises compliance complexity.
  - Anti‑corruption (FCPA) and competition law exposure; sanctions/export/import controls and evolving trade regimes (e.g., impacts from geopolitical conflicts) may restrict operations.
  - Expanding data and digital regulations (GDPR, DPF, DMA/DSA, Data Act) and potential telecom, ESG, cybersecurity, accessibility, and AI rules increase cost and uncertainty; noncompliance could lead to fines and restrictions.
  - Ongoing claims and lawsuits carry financial and injunctive risks; government contracting adds audit, funding, and termination risks.
  - Tax uncertainties from audits (including transfer pricing), legislative changes, mix of international earnings, and evolving global tax rules.
- Intellectual property risks:
  - Challenges protecting IP globally; changing patent landscapes; open-source obligations; risks from source code leaks; third-party infringement claims may lead to costs, redesigns, or sales limits.
- General risks:
  - Brand/reputation harm from privacy, security, product, or policy issues amplified by social media.
  - Macroeconomic pressures (inflation, recession) impacting IT/PC demand and partners; credit risks and investment portfolio sensitivity (including to U.S. credit rating).
  - Catastrophic events, pandemics, climate impacts on energy/cooling, and geopolitical instability (e.g., conflicts) may disrupt operations and supply chains.
  - Global operations risks: currency volatility, nationalism/protectionism, trade restrictions; talent attraction/retention, immigration limits, unionization trends, and succession planning.
- Item 1B: No unresolved SEC staff comments as of FY2023.
- Item 2 (Properties): Corporate HQ in Redmond, WA; total 78 million sq. ft. of space (U.S.: 47M; International: 31M); 36M owned, 42M leased; ongoing consolidation of office leases; additional owned/leased offices, R&D sites, and datacenters worldwide.
- Item 3 (Legal Proceedings): Referenced in financial statement notes.
- Item 4 (Mine Safety): Not applicable.

It notes that Microsoft’s common stock trades on NASDAQ under the symbol MSFT and had 83,883 registered holders of record as of July 24, 2023. The company repurchased 14,777,254 shares in Q4 FY23 across April–June 2023 at average prices of $287.97, $314.26, and $334.15, respectively, using cash resources via open-market purchases and/or a Rule 10b5-1 plan; these figures exclude shares repurchased to cover employee tax withholding. - Fiscal 2023 highlights vs. 2022:

structure.title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.heading: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase:
The following Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations (“MD&A”) is intended to help the reader

understand the results of operations and financial condition of Microsoft Corporation.
structure.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) for Microsoft’s fiscal year ended June 30, 2023, comparing results to fiscal 2022, with references to prior-year MD&A for 2022 vs. 2021.
- Company overview: Mission, AI-driven platforms and tools, revenue model (cloud, software licensing, advertising, devices), and major cost drivers.
- FY23 business highlights: Strong Microsoft Cloud growth (+22% to $111.6B); Office Commercial (+10% with Office 365 Commercial +13%); Office Consumer (+2%, 67.0M subscribers); LinkedIn (+10%); Dynamics (+16% with Dynamics 365 +24%); Server and cloud services (+19% with Azure +29%); Windows OEM (-25%); Devices (-24%); Windows Commercial (+5%); Xbox content/services (-3%); Search and news advertising ex-TAC (+11%).
- Industry dynamics: Rapid technology and business model shifts; competitive landscape; R&D focus aligned to customer needs and trends.
- Macro environment and risks: Global demand sensitivity to macro/geopolitical factors; rising cloud/AI infrastructure and device costs; data center capacity constraints (land, power, networking, GPUs); supply chain considerations; talent attraction/retention; foreign exchange impacts (FY23 FX headwinds on revenue/expenses).
- Cost alignment actions: Q2 FY23 $1.2B charge (employee severance, hardware portfolio impairments, lease consolidation); ~10,000 role reductions; continued hiring in strategic areas; real estate optimization.
- Seasonality: Revenue generally higher in Q2 (holiday/corporate spend) and Q4 (multi-year on-premises contracts).
- Accounting estimate change: Server and network equipment useful lives extended from 4 to 6 years (effective FY23), increasing FY23 operating income by $3.7B and net income by $3.0B ($0.40 per share).
- Segment reporting and performance metrics: Three segments—Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, More Personal Computing; updated metrics (e.g., broader Devices metric); definitions of key commercial and segment metrics, including Microsoft Cloud revenue and gross margin percentage.
- Consolidated results (FY23 vs. FY22): Revenue $211.9B (+7%); gross margin $146.1B (+8%); operating income $88.5B (+6%); net income $72.4B (-1%); diluted EPS $9.68 (flat). Non-GAAP measures adjust for the Q2 charge in FY23 and a prior-year tax benefit; FX headwinds on revenue, gross margin, operating income; Q2 charge’s negative impact on profitability metrics.
- Segment results:
  - Productivity and Business Processes: Revenue +9%; Office 365 Commercial seats +11%; LinkedIn strength in Talent Solutions; operating income +15%; FX headwinds.
  - Intelligent Cloud: Revenue +17% (Azure +29% consumption-led growth); Enterprise Services +4%; operating income +14%; margin pressures from mix shift to Azure; investments (including Nuance) and severance costs; FX headwinds.
  - More Personal Computing: Revenue -9% (Windows OEM -25%, Devices -24%, Gaming -5%; Search/news +5% or +11% ex-TAC with Xandr); operating income -20%; margin declines in Devices; FX headwinds.
- Operating expenses: 
  - R&D +11% (cloud engineering, LinkedIn).
  - Sales & Marketing +4% (Nuance, Xandr, commercial sales; lower Windows advertising).
  - G&A +28% (severance; Irish DPC-related charge).
- Other income (expense), net: Higher interest income (yields), lower interest expense (debt maturities), lower gains on investments, higher derivative losses tied to strategic investments, FX remeasurement gains.
- Income taxes: Effective tax rate 19% (vs. 13% prior year due to FY22 $3.3B intangible transfer tax benefit and lower stock-based comp benefits); U.S. vs. foreign income mix; ongoing IRS audits (2004–2017) with unresolved transfer pricing matters; adequate tax contingency allowances.
- Non-GAAP reconciliations: Adjusted gross margin, operating income, net income, and EPS excluding Q2 FY23 charge and prior-year intangible transfer tax benefit.
- Liquidity and capital resources: Strong liquidity (cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments $111.3B); investment portfolio composition and valuation approach (Level 1/2 predominance); cash flow drivers (operations, financing, investing) and year-over-year changes.
- Debt and capital structure: Use of debt for general corporate purposes; summary of maturities and interest; unearned revenue balance ($53.8B) and recognition schedule.
- Material cash requirements: Long-term debt service, construction commitments (data centers), leases, and purchase commitments (notably data center-related).
- Taxes payable: TCJA transition tax remaining ($10.5B over next three years; $2.7B within 12 months); FY23 cash tax impact from mandatory R&D capitalization.
- Capital returns: Share repurchases ($18.4B FY23; $22.3B authorization remaining of $60B program); dividends ($20.2B FY23; intent to continue).
- Strategic investments: Pending acquisition of Activision Blizzard; merger agreement extended to October 18, 2023; continued investment in cloud and AI infrastructure; expectation of higher capex to support AI and cloud growth.
- Critical accounting estimates: Revenue recognition (multi-element arrangements, SSP judgments), impairment of investment securities, goodwill impairment testing, software development capitalization, legal contingencies, income taxes (uncertain positions), and inventory valuation.
- Governance and controls: Management’s responsibility statement; internal control environment; independent audit by Deloitte & Touche LLP; Audit Committee oversight.
- Market risk disclosures (Item 7A): Exposure to foreign currency, interest rate, credit, and equity risks; use of derivatives to manage exposures; sensitivity analysis illustrating potential impacts on earnings and fair value.

structure.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk
structure.heading: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk
structure.start_phrase: We are exposed to economic risk from foreign exchange rates, interest rates, credit risk, and equity prices.
structure.summary:
- Quantitative and qualitative market risk disclosures (Item 7A):
  - The company is exposed to risks from foreign exchange rates, interest rates, credit, and equity prices and uses derivative instruments to manage, but not eliminate, these exposures.
  - Foreign currency risk: exposures on forecasted transactions, assets, and liabilities; positions (including hedges) are monitored daily for economic effectiveness. Key currencies: Euro, Japanese yen, British pound, Canadian dollar, and Australian dollar.
  - Interest rate risk: fixed‑income portfolio managed by adjusting average maturity to align economic returns with global fixed‑income indices.
  - Credit risk: diversified, primarily investment‑grade fixed‑income holdings; credit exposures managed relative to broad‑based indices.
  - Equity price risk: equity investment portfolio subject to market price fluctuations.
  - Sensitivity analysis (potential loss from hypothetical changes, in millions):
    - Foreign currency – Revenue: 10% decrease in FX rates → $(8,122) impact to earnings.
    - Foreign currency – Investments: 10% decrease in FX rates → $(29) impact to fair value.
    - Interest rate: +100 bps in U.S. Treasury rates → $(1,832) impact to fair value.
    - Credit: +100 bps in credit spreads → $(354) impact to fair value.
    - Equity: 10% decrease in equity market prices → $(705) impact to earnings.

- Financial statements and supplementary data (Item 8) – Consolidated income statements (in millions, except per share):
  - Revenue:
    - Product: $64,699 (2023), $72,732 (2022), $71,074 (2021)
    - Service and other: $147,216 (2023), $125,538 (2022), $97,014 (2021)
    - Total: $211,915 (2023), $198,270 (2022), $168,088 (2021)
  - Cost of revenue: $65,863 (2023), $62,650 (2022), $52,232 (2021)
  - Gross margin: $146,052 (2023), $135,620 (2022), $115,856 (2021)
  - Operating expenses:
    - Research and development: $27,195 (2023), $24,512 (2022), $20,716 (2021)
    - Sales and marketing: $22,759 (2023), $21,825 (2022), $20,117 (2021)
    - General and administrative: $7,575 (2023), $5,900 (2022), $5,107 (2021)
  - Operating income: $88,523 (2023), $83,383 (2022), $69,916 (2021)
  - Other income, net: $788 (2023), $333 (2022), $1,186 (2021)
  - Income before income taxes: $89,311 (2023), $83,716 (2022), $71,102 (2021)
  - Provision for income taxes: $16,950 (2023), $10,978 (2022), $9,831 (2021)
  - Net income: $72,361 (2023), $72,738 (2022), $61,271 (2021)
  - Earnings per share:
    - Basic: $9.72 (2023), $9.70 (2022), $8.12 (2021)
    - Diluted: $9.68 (2023), $9.65 (2022), $8.05 (2021)
  - Weighted average shares outstanding:
    - Basic: 7,446 (2023), 7,496 (2022), 7,547 (2021)
    - Diluted: 7,472 (2023), 7,540 (2022), 7,608 (2021)

- Notable trends highlighted by the data:
  - Total revenue grew year over year, driven by increases in service and other revenue, while product revenue declined in 2023 versus 2022.
  - Gross margin and operating income increased each year.
  - Net income was roughly flat in 2023 versus 2022, with slightly higher EPS due to a lower share count.

structure.title: Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
structure.heading: Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
structure.start_phrase: Refer to accompanying notes.
structure.summary:
- Scope: Item 8 (Financial Statements and Supplementary Data) from Microsoft’s Form 10-K, including primary financial statements for FY2023, FY2022, FY2021; changes in stockholders’ equity; comprehensive income; notes to the financial statements; auditor’s report; and controls and procedures.

- Key FY2023 results:
  - Revenue $211.9B (Product $64.7B; Service & other $147.2B); gross margin $146.1B.
  - Operating income $88.5B; net income $72.4B; diluted EPS $9.68; weighted-average diluted shares 7.47B.
  - Comprehensive income $70.7B (OCI loss driven by investment valuation and FX).
  - Cash from operations $87.6B; cash used in investing $(22.7)B; cash used in financing $(43.9)B; ending cash & equivalents $34.7B.
  - Balance sheet: total assets $412.0B (cash, cash equivalents & short-term investments $111.3B; PP&E, net $95.6B; goodwill $67.9B); total liabilities $205.8B (current $104.1B; long-term debt $42.0B); stockholders’ equity $206.2B.

- Capital allocation:
  - Share repurchases: 69M shares for $18.4B in FY2023; $22.3B remaining under $60B authorization (no expiration).
  - Dividends declared: $2.72 per share ($20.2B).
  - Capex: additions to PP&E $(28.1)B; PP&E net increased to $95.6B; committed $13.5B (primarily datacenters).

- Significant accounting policies and estimates:
  - GAAP basis; consolidation; extensive revenue recognition disclosures (performance obligations, SSP, variable consideration, multi-element arrangements).
  - Change in useful lives for server and network equipment from 4 to 6 years (effective FY2023) increased FY2023 operating income by $3.7B and net income by $3.0B (~$0.40 per share).
  - Allowance for doubtful accounts activity; financing receivables; costs to obtain a contract; stock-based compensation (RSUs/PSUs), ESPP.

- Investments, fair value, and derivatives:
  - Debt securities AFS with unrealized losses primarily from interest rates; equity investments (Level 1 and others).
  - Derivative programs for FX, interest rate, equity, and credit risk; notional amounts disclosed; fair value hierarchy; hedge accounting impacts and gains/losses.

- Inventories and PP&E:
  - Inventories $2.5B (down from $3.7B).
  - PP&E components detailed; FY2023 depreciation $11.0B (decline due to useful life change).

- Business combinations and pending acquisition:
  - Nuance (closed March 2022): purchase price ~$18.8B; goodwill to Intelligent Cloud; identifiable intangibles and lives disclosed.
  - ZeniMax (closed March 2021): ~$8.1B; goodwill to More Personal Computing.
  - Activision Blizzard: signed January 2022 for $68.7B; pending regulatory approvals; merger agreement extended to October 18, 2023.

- Goodwill and intangibles:
  - Goodwill $67.9B across segments; no impairments identified in annual tests; accumulated goodwill impairment $11.3B.
  - Finite-lived intangibles net $9.4B; amortization expense $2.5B; future amortization schedule provided.

- Debt:
  - Total face value $52.9B; long-term debt (net) $42.0B; maturities schedule provided; interest paid $1.7B; fair value ~$46.2B.

- Income taxes:
  - Provision $17.0B; ETR 19.0% (benefits from foreign earnings at lower rates, FDII, R&D credit; offset by interest and other items).
  - Notable items: FY2022 intangible property transfer to U.S. yielded $3.3B tax benefit; FY2021 India Supreme Court decision on software withholding taxes ($620M benefit).
  - Deferred tax assets/liabilities detailed (including TCJA-required capitalization of R&D beginning FY2023); net DTA $19.7B.
  - Uncertain tax positions $17.1B (primarily transfer pricing with IRS); interest accrued $5.2B; long-running IRS audits (2004–2017) unresolved.

- Unearned revenue and RPO:
  - Unearned revenue $53.8B (by segment disclosed).
  - Remaining performance obligations ~$229B (≈45% to be recognized within 12 months).

- Leases:
  - Operating lease ROU assets $14.3B; finance lease assets (PP&E, net) $15.9B; total lease liabilities: operating $15.1B, finance $17.1B.
  - Lease costs and cash flows disclosed; significant not-yet-commenced leases for datacenters (operating ~$7.7B; finance ~$34.4B).

- Contingencies:
  - U.S. cell phone litigation (radio frequency emission claims) – court excluded plaintiffs’ general causation experts (April 2023).
  - Irish DPC preliminary draft decision on LinkedIn targeted advertising under GDPR; Microsoft intends to challenge.
  - Legal accruals $617M; reasonably possible additional losses up to ~$600M beyond recorded amounts.

- Equity and employee plans:
  - Shares outstanding 7.432B at FY2023 end; detailed repurchase activity by quarter.
  - Stock-based compensation expense $9.6B; unrecognized comp cost $18.6B (≈3-year weighted average); ESPP purchases (7M shares).

- Segment and geographic information:
  - Segments: Productivity & Business Processes (revenue $69.3B; op income $34.2B), Intelligent Cloud ($87.9B; $37.9B), More Personal Computing ($54.7B; $16.5B).
  - Microsoft Cloud revenue $111.6B (Azure, Office 365 Commercial, LinkedIn commercial, Dynamics 365).
  - Revenue by product/service (e.g., Server & cloud $80.0B; Office $48.7B; Windows $21.5B; Gaming $15.5B; LinkedIn $15.1B; Search & news $12.2B; Devices $5.5B; Dynamics $5.4B).
  - Geographic revenue roughly half U.S./half other countries; long-lived assets concentrated in U.S. and Ireland.

- Auditor’s report and controls:
  - Deloitte & Touche LLP issued unqualified opinions on the financial statements and internal control over financial reporting.
  - Critical audit matters: revenue recognition judgments (multi-element arrangements, SSP) and uncertain tax positions (transfer pricing).
  - Management concluded disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting were effective; no material changes in Q4 FY2023.

structure.start_phrase: The financial statements are set forth under Part II, Item 8 of this Form 10-K, as indexed below.
structure.summary: Part IV, Item 15 of Microsoft’s Form 10-K outlines the company’s financial statements and exhibits. It provides an index to the financial statements included in Part II, Item 8—covering Income Statements, Comprehensive Income, Balance Sheets, Cash Flows, Stockholders’ Equity, Notes, and the Report of the Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm—with page references (approximately pages 58–96), and notes that financial statement schedules are omitted as not required or included elsewhere. It also lists exhibits, largely incorporated by reference, including the Amended and Restated Articles of Incorporation, Bylaws, a 2009 base indenture, and supplemental indentures for various note issuances, with corresponding prior SEC filing forms and dates (e.g., Forms 8-K and S-3ASR).

structure.title: Exhibit and Financial Statement Schedules
structure.heading: Item 15. Exhibit and Financial Statement Schedules
structure.start_phrase: The financial statements are set forth under Part II, Item 8 of this Form 10-K, as indexed below.
structure.summary:
- Part IV, Item 15 outlines Exhibits and Financial Statement Schedules. It states the audited financial statements are included in Part II, Item 8 and provides an index with page numbers for Income Statements, Comprehensive Income Statements, Balance Sheets, Cash Flow Statements, Stockholders’ Equity Statements, Notes, and the Independent Auditor’s Report. Financial statement schedules are omitted as not required, not applicable, or included elsewhere.
- A comprehensive Exhibit Listing is provided, largely incorporated by reference, covering:
  - Corporate governance documents (Amended and Restated Articles of Incorporation; Bylaws).
  - Debt instruments (base indenture and numerous supplemental indentures for various note issuances from 2009–2021).
  - Description of securities.
  - Management and compensatory plans/agreements (2001 and 2017 stock plans; employee stock purchase plan; performance and stock award agreement forms; deferred compensation plans, including for non-employee directors; executive incentive and severance plans).
  - Indemnification agreements and related trust agreements for officers and directors.
  - Executive offer letters (e.g., Satya Nadella; Christopher Young).
- Exhibits filed with this report include the list of subsidiaries (Exhibit 21), auditor consent (23.1), CEO/CFO Section 302 certifications (31.1, 31.2), CEO/CFO Section 906 certifications noted as furnished, not filed (32.1, 32.2), and Inline XBRL exhibits (101 series) including the cover page (104).
- Notations: an asterisk identifies management contracts or compensatory plans; a double asterisk indicates exhibits furnished, not filed.
- Part IV, Item 16 states there is no Form 10-K Summary.

structure.title: Signatures
structure.heading: Signatures
structure.start_phrase:
Pursuant to the requirements of Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, the Registrant has duly caused this report to be signed on its
 
behalf by the undersigned; thereunto duly authorized, in the City of Redmond, State of Washington, on July 27, 2023.
structure.summary:
- Signature pages for Microsoft Corporation’s FY2023 Form 10-K, executed July 27, 2023 in Redmond, WA, including corporate signature by the Principal Accounting Officer and signatures of the CEO (Principal Executive Officer), CFO (Principal Financial Officer), Lead Independent Director, and other directors.
- Exhibit 21: List of significant subsidiaries as of June 30, 2023, including key entities in Ireland and the United States (e.g., Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited, Microsoft Global Finance, Microsoft Online, Inc., LinkedIn Corporation and its Irish affiliate, Nuance Communications, Inc.), with immaterial subsidiaries omitted.
- Exhibit 23.1: Deloitte & Touche LLP’s consent to the incorporation by reference of their audit reports into certain Microsoft Form S-8 and Form S-3 registration statements, dated July 27, 2023.
- Exhibits 31.1 and 31.2: Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 certifications by the CEO (Satya Nadella) and CFO (Amy E. Hood) attesting to the accuracy of the 10-K, fair presentation of financials, and the design, evaluation, and disclosure of disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting, including acknowledgment of responsibilities for reporting deficiencies and fraud to auditors/audit committee.
- Exhibits 32.1 and 32.2: Sarbanes-Oxley Section 906 certifications by the CEO and CFO stating that the 10-K complies with Exchange Act reporting requirements and fairly presents the Company’s financial condition and results, with notice that signed originals are retained and available to the SEC upon request.
